text: RESEARCH ARTICLE www.advenergymat.de Tuning Polysulfides into Clustered-States via Non-coordinating Molecular Encapsulation to Achieve an Alternative Kinetics in Li─S Batteries Qingyi Zheng, Leyuan Cui, Xiaojiao Zhao, Ruming Yuan, Chutao Wang, Kun Wang, Jingmin Fan, Mingsen Zheng,* and Quanfeng Dong* The practical application of lithium–sulfur batteries is hindered by the polysulfide shuttle effect and sluggish kinetics inherent in solid–liquid–solid conversion mechanism, particularly under lean electrolyte conditions (<5 μL mg−1).

Weakly solvating electrolytes and localized high-concentration electrolytes can suppress polysulfide dissolution and enable a quasi-solid- -phase mechanism but suffer from severely limited reaction kinetics.
Herein, a clustered-polysulfide-mediated sulfur conversion mechanism enabled by a novel electrolyte composed of 1,2-dimethylbenzene (DTL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) is proposed.

The encapsulation effect of DTL and the coordination of TFSI−with polysulfides drives the aggregation of polysulfides so that the clustered polysulfides with virtual shell boundaries can be the new basic reactive that bridges the gap between the traditional dissolution-dominated mechanism and quasi-solid-state mechanism.

The clustered polysulfide electrolyte (CPE) not only suppresses the shuttle effect and stabilizes the lithium anode by mitigating parasitic reactions but also enables alternative reaction kinetics and promotes 3D Li2S deposition, minimizing electrode passivation.
Ultimately, lithium–sulfur batteries can achieve excellent electrochemical performance and can stably operate under lean electrolyte- (<4.0 μL mg−1) with an area capacity of >4 mAh cm−2.
This work elucidates the relationship between polysulfide dissolution behavior and redox kinetics, providing a new insight into the understanding of complex sulfur conversion mechanisms. 1.
Introduction Lithium–sulfur batteries (Li─S batteries) are expected to be one of the next-generation high-energy-density energy storage Q.

engineering, aiming to balance polysulfide dissolution suppression with kinetic optimization.[7] Weakly solvating electrolytes (such as fluorinated ethers,[8] monoether solvents[9]) and localized conversion mechanism.[11] This approach effectively decouples reaction kinetics from polysulfide dissolution, demonstrating promising performance under lean electrolyte conditions.[12] However, the use of high concentrations of lithium salts with fluorinated solvents significantly increases the cost and density of the electrolyte.[13] More fatally, the quasi-solid phase conversion mechanism Current strategies for weakly solvating electrolytes primarily focus on suppressing polysulfide solubility,[6b] but the regulatory mechanism of dynamic polysulfide dissolution states on the cathode sulfur reaction remains rarely explored.

Herein, guided by the idea of regulating the state of reactive species, we developed a novel electrolyte with low salt concentration (1 mol L−1) and low density (1.1 g cm−3) by employing 1,2- dimethylbenzene (DTL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) as solvents and achieved a clustered polysulfides-mediated sulfur conversion mechanism.

The encapsulation effect of DTL with the ligand-mediated action of bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI−) drives the formation of polysulfide clusters in the electrolyte, thus realizing a clustered polysulfide encapsulation mechanism intermediate between the conventional solidliquid dissolution mechanism and the quasi-solid-solid conversion mechanism.

Clustered polysulfide electrolyte (CPE) not only significantly suppresses polysulfide solubility but also optimizes Li2S deposition behavior, guiding the formation of 3D Li2S particles that minimize conductive electrode coverage.
Furthermore, the CPE effectively mitigates side reactions between polysulfides and lithium metal, thereby stabilizing the Li anode interface.

As a result, the lithium–sulfur batteries exhibit exceptional reaction kinetics and electrochemical reversibility, achieving a remarkable coulombic efficiency of 99.6% and delivering a high capacity of 718 mAh g−1 at 5 C.

Moreover, the batteries can stably operate under lean electrolyte conditions with electrolyte-to-sulfur ratio (E/S) < 4.0 μL mg−1, highlighting its potential for practical highenergy-density applications. 2.
Results and Discussion 2.1.

Construction of CPE Electrolyte Figure 1a and Table S1 (Supporting Information) compared the donor number (DN) and dielectric constants (ɛ) of a broader range of common solvents, ranging from low DN/ɛ to high DN/ɛ.[16] Conventional ether solvents for lithium–sulfur batteries such as 1,2-Dimethoxymethane (DME, DN = 20.0, ɛ = 5.5), 1,3-Dioxane (DOL, DN = 21.3, ɛ = 7.3) have medium DN values and ɛ, indicating good solvation ability with lithium ions.

In addition, a series of solvents with high DN values and ɛ (DMA, DN = 27.8, ɛ = 7.3; TMU, DN = 23.4, ɛ = 31.2; DMSO, DN = 46.7, ɛ = 29.8) are shown in the upper right corner, where higher solvation capacity can further promote the solubility of polysulfides.[17] In the lower-left corner, we have listed a series of potential non-coordinating solvents, including DTL (DN = 0.1, ɛ = 2.6), Heptance (HPT, DN = 0.0, ɛ = 1.9), Cyclohexane (CYH, DN = 0.0, ɛ = 2.0), Benzene (DN = 0.1, ɛ = 2.3), and Toluene (TL, DN = 0.1, ɛ = 2.4).

The minimum electrostatic potentials (ESPmin) of DTL and other ether solvents were calculated, as shown in Figure 1b.
Higher ESPmin and more dispersed charges of DTL suggest that the coordination between DTL and lithium-ion is difficult.
Due to its weakly polar nature, DTL induces phase separation between DME and DTL when the DTL content exceeds 60%.

Therefore, a 5% volume fraction of tetrahydrofuran (THF) was added to the electrolyte to form a homogeneous and stable solution.[11a] The electrolyte formulations with different DTL contents are shown in Table S2 (Supporting Information).

Specifically, 1 mol L−1 lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) was dissolved in the mixture solution of DME/THF = 95/5 (v/v) and DME/THF/DTL = 35/5/60 (v/v), denoted as 0DTL electrolyte and 60DTL electrolyte, respectively.
The numbers represent the volume fraction of DTL in electrolytes.
The dissolution of polysulfides is closely related to the shuttle effect in lithium–sulfur batteries.
The solubility of sulfur atoms in different electrolytes was determined by the Li2S6 dissolution experiment.
As shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), lithium polysulfides are completely insoluble in pure DTL solvent and the solution still appears clear and transparent.
In contrast, lithium polysulfides dissolved heavily in 0DTL and the solution appeared dark black.
With DTL content increasing, the solubility of lithium polysulfide decreases and the color gradually changes from dark black to red.
UV–vis spectroscopy was further performed to obtain the solubility of polysulfides in different electrolytes, as shown in Figure 1c.
As shown in Table S3 (Supporting Information), the solubility of sulfur atoms in 50DTL, 60DTL, and 70DTL was 305, 247, and 101 mmol L−1, respectively.

Among them, the sulfur solubility of 60DTL is only ≈5% of that in conventional ether electrolytes (4000 mmol L−1).[2d] Consequently, the dissolution of polysulfides is significantly reduced due to the reduced electrolyte solvating capacity after introducing DTL.
To reveal the driving effect of the DTL, the 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Raman spectroscopy were performed to examine the different electrolytes with 1 mol L−1 LiTFSI as lithium salt.

Raman spectra show that the C─O─C vibration peak of free DME molecules at 847 cm−1 diminishes with the increasing volume fraction of DTL from 0% to 80% (Figure S2, Supporting Information), indicating a decrease in the free DME solvents and an increase in the liganded DME solvents.
As shown in Figure 1d, the coordination of lithium ions with TFSI−anions is enhanced with increasing DTL volume fraction.
It leads to an increase in the electron cloud density of lithium atoms and an increase in the shielding effect, which in turn leads to a decrease in the chemical shift of 7Li NMR.
The 7Li NMR peak exhibits the lowest chemical shift when the DTL content is 50–60%.
In this case, the strongest encapsulation effect of DTL can drive aggregation of TFSI−and Li+.

However, excessive DTL molecules (>60%, v/v) make insufficient solvents for coordination with lithium ions, instead destroying the coordination environment of lithium ions, which in turn results in an increase in the chemical shift of 7Li peak.

Similarly, the electrolyte with Li2S6 as the only lithium salt also shows a decreasing chemical shift of 7Li peak with increasing DTL content, further demonstrating the driving effect of DTL (Figure S3, Supporting Information). 2.2.
Clustered-Polysulfides Species in CPE In lithium–sulfur batteries, lithium polysulfide intermediates possess important roles in the sulfur reduction reaction.
As shown in Figure 2a, lithium polysulfides tend to exist as a single neutral molecule in the 0DTL electrolyte (conventional ether electrolyte, noted as CE).
In this work, by the driving effect of DTL, the polysulfides were allowed to aggregate in CPE and form cluster species with the mediation of TFSI−.
As a result, polysulfides no longer exist as a free molecule, but form a cluster state molecule aggregated in CPE, as shown in Figure 2b,c.
Machine learning potentials for molecular dynamics (MLMD) simulation were performed to reveal the CPE mechanism.

Recently, Liu et al. revealed that Li2S4 is the key species that determines the kinetics of sulfur reduction reaction.[19] So the shortchain Li2S4 was chosen as the typical polysulfide species because it is the only liquid phase species for the liquid-solid conversion process (Li2S4→Li2S) and largely determines the kinetics of sulfur reduction reaction.
Snapshots of the two electrolytes with Li2S4 molecules are shown in Figure 2d,e.
In CE, the Li2S4 exists as typical neutral molecules.
In contrast, the Li2S4 molecules in CPE are aggregated to form cluster-state species.

Figures S4 and S5, (Supporting Information) show the localized simulated snapshots of CE and CPE, demonstrating the conversion of active species from single-molecule Li2S4 to clustered Li2S4 species in 60DTL electrolyte.

In addition, the stretching central S─S bond of Li2S4 in CPE species was observed (from 1.95–2.45 to 2.45– 2.85 Å), suggesting that the clustered polysulfide species have a stronger reactivity than polysulfides (Figure S5, Supporting Information).
A sharp peak of Li (Li2S4)─O (TFSI) appeared within the solvent sheath layer at 2.5Å in CPE (Figure 2f).
The coordination number of Li (Li2S4)─O (TFSI) in the CPE electrolyte was increased from 0 to 0.72, indicating that polysulfides are agglomerated under the mediation of TFSI−.
In contrast, the radial distribution plots around Li atom of Li2S4 molecules indicate that only DME or THF molecules are present within the solvated sheath of Li2S4 at 2.5 Å in CE (Figure 2g).
Also, as shown in Figure S6 (Supporting Information), the radial distribution plots around Li+ of LiTFSI molecules reveal a significantly enhanced ship peak of Li(TFSI)-S(Li2S4) in CPE.

The 19F and 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were performed to verify the formation of cluster species. 20 mmol L−1 Li2S4 or Li2S6 was added to the CE and CPE electrolyte with 1 mol L−1 LiTFSI.

As shown in Figure 2h,i, the 19F peak of CE electrolyte was hardly shifted after adding lithium polysulfides, which suggests that polysulfide species are present as free molecules and have not entered the solvated sheath of TFSI−.
In contrast, the 19F peak of CPE exhibits a pronounced increased chemical shift (≈0.2 ppm), which directly evidences the formation of a cluster state between polysulfides and TFSI−.

In addition, after introducing LiTFSI, the 7Li peak of CPE shows a more significantly reduced chemical shift, suggesting that TFSI− promotes the formation of clustered polysulfide species (Figure S8b, Supporting Information).
The new small absorption in UV– vis spectra of CPE with Li2S6 also supports the above observation (Figure S9, Supporting Information).
Figure S10 (Supporting Information) shows the Raman spectra of CPE with and without Li2S6.
When Li2S6 was introduced into the CPE system containing LiTFSI, the S─N─S vibrational peak of TFSI−blue shifted.

This originates from the synergistic coordination between TFSI− and polysulfides during the formation of cluster state molecules: Li+ forms a 3D structure by bridging the oxygen atoms of TFSI− and the sulfur atoms of the polysulfides, and this rigid coordination environment results in the restricted vibrational degrees of freedom of the S─N─S bonds and an increase in the chemical bond force constant (k) increases, which ultimately leads to an increase in the vibrational frequency.[20] The Raman results agree with molecular dynamics simulations and NMR results, which together demonstrate the formation of cluster polysulfides driven by TFSI−.

Impact of CPE Species on Deposition Behavior in Sulfur Reduction Reaction The Li─Li2S6 cells were assembled to investigate the effect of the CPE mechanism on the sulfur conversion process.
The same concentration of Li2S6 was used as the active species to exclude the influence of polysulfide solubility on reaction kinetics.

The cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of Li─Li2S6 cells show that the initial reduction peak potential (corresponding to S8 to Li2S4) gradually reduced and the second reduction peak potential (corresponding to Li2S4 to Li2S) increased with increasing DTL content (Figure 3a).
In comparison with the 0DTL electrolyte, the second reduction peak potential was increased from 1.971 to 2.012 V in 60DTL electrolyte.

Potentiostatic-intermittent titration technique (PITT) was further performed to reveal the Li2S deposition behavior.[21] As shown in Figure 3b,c, the PITT curves of the Li─Li2S8 cells appear an obvious broad peak with a gradual decrease of voltage, which corresponds to the deposition process of Li2S4 to Li2S.
The Li2S nucleation potential was elevated from 2.04 to 2.08 V in the CPE electrolyte.
The deposition kinetic behavior was revealed by quantitative peak fitting to the current-time transient curves.

The deposition process of Li2S can be categorized into four classical models: 2D progressive nucleation (2DP), 2D instantaneous nucleation (2DI), 3D progressive nucleation (3DP), and 3D instantaneous nucleation (3DI).
The deposition of polysulfides to lithium sulfide is divided into nucleation and growth.

The nucleation process follows below: N = N0 (1 −exp (−At)) (1) where N represents the nuclei density on a certain substrate, t is the given time, N0 represents the density of available nucleation sites, and A is the nucleation rate.
When the nucleation rate A is large, Li2S nuclei are formed rapidly in a short period, which is called instantaneous nucleation.
When A is small, the nucleation density increases linearly with time, which is called progressive nucleation.

The growth process of Li2S is controlled by the diffusion of active species, which can be divided into 2D deposition and 3D deposition according to the different control steps.[22] As shown in Figure 3d,e, the Li2S deposition is well matched with the 3DP model in the CPE electrolyte, while it is situated between the 2DP and 2DI models in the CE electrolyte.

The 3D deposition model allows cells to release higher capacity and avoids premature end of discharge process caused by insulating Li2S covering the electrode surface.[23] Meanwhile, the Li2S deposition process in different electrolytes was compared by chronoamperometry experiment at 2.08 V.
As shown in Figure 3f, the deposition process in 0DTL electrolyte could not proceed due to the large overpotential.
With the increasing DTL content, the deposition peak appeared and gradually advanced, indicating that the Li2S deposition kinetics gradually accelerated.
The highest deposition capacity of Li2S (434 mAh g−1) was observed in 60DTL electrolytes, which is consistent with the results of CV experiments.
The scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of Li2S deposited on carbon paper are shown in Figure 3g–j.

In 0DTL electrolytes, small lithium sulfide particles can be observed in the middle of discharge, and moss-like lithium sulfide can also be observed in some areas, which corresponds to the 2D deposition mode of lithium sulfide (Figure 3i).

In 60DTL electrolytes, due to the change of deposition mode (2D to 3D), the lithium sulfide can grow along the 3D direction, forming large-sized lithium sulfide in the form of liquid droplets (Figure 3g).

Ultimately, a 3D lithium sulfide deposition morphology can be realized in a 60DTL electrolyte (Figure 3h), while the mossy lithium sulfide in a 0DTL electrolyte grows into a film-like lithium sulfide and completely covers the conductive electrode (Figure 3j).
Figure S12 (Supporting Information) also shows the Li2S deposition morphology for electrolytes with different DTL contents.
Consequently, the deposition morphology of lithium sulfide can be modulated by the clustered polysulfides. 2.4.
Sulfur Redox Reaction Mediated by CPE The charge/discharge curves of Li─S cells in 0DTL and 60DTL electrolytes are shown in Figure 4a.
The behavior of a chargedischarge process is different, especially in the initial stage.

In Li─S batteries, the first discharge plateau corresponds to the conversion of sulfur to long-chain polysulfides, while the second discharge plateau corresponds to the conversion of polysulfides to lithium sulfide.
The tilted region between the first and second plateaus corresponds to the conversion of dissolved long-chain polysulfides to short-chain polysulfides.
The decrease in polysulfide solubility and the change in the state of reactive species caused the sulfur reaction to intermediate between the liquid and “quasi-solid” reactions.
Therefore, the voltage of the first discharge plateau decreases from 2.35 to 2.2 V in 60DTL electrolyte, accompanied by a significant decrease in the capacity of the tilted region.
In addition, significantly higher capacity and increased voltage of the second platform in 60DTL electrolyte indicate that the reduction process from Li2S4 to Li2S is effectively promoted.
During the charge process, two voltage platforms exist in 0DTL electrolyte, corresponding to the conversion of lithium sulfide to polysulfides and polysulfides to sulfur.
In contrast, only one voltage plateau exists in 60DTL electrolytes, indicating that CPE species also change the reaction mechanism of the charging process.
The initial specific capacity of Li─S cells with 60DTL electrolyte was increased from 1002 to 1371 mAh g−1 at 0.1 C, and the overpotential was reduced from 173 to 116 mV.
It is noteworthy that the coulombic efficiency of cells with 60DTL electrolyte is increased from 76.3% to 99.6% due to the effective inhibition of the shuttle effect.
Charge–discharge curves for the first two cycles of electrolyte with different DTL content (0%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, v/v) and DOL/DME electrolyte are also shown in Figure S13 (Supporting Information).
A significant decrease in the first discharge plateau was observed at DTL contents of 50–80%.
The overpotential, discharge capacity, coulombic efficiency, and Q2/Q1 (capacity ratio of two discharge plateaus) of different electrolytes were further compared (Figure S14, Supporting Information).
Cells with 60DTL electrolyte have the lowest overpotential and highest discharge capacity (Figure S14b,c, Supporting Information).
Compared with 0DTL electrolyte, the value of Q2/Q1 of 60DTL electrolyte increases from 2.27 to 2.86, indicating a more complete deposition of Li2S (Figure S14d, Supporting Information).
Q2/Q1 in 70 DTL and 80 DTL electrolytes even exceeded the theoretical values (Q2/Q1 = 3).

As shown in Figure 4b, the peak potential and onset potential of the second reduction peak (R2) for cells with 60DTL electrolyte were significantly advanced from 1.96 to 2.05 and 2.06 to 2.12 V, and the peak current was also increased.

The oxidation peak (O1) of cells with 60TL turned from a large broad peak to a sharp peak, with a reduced peak potential (2.52 to 2.45 V) and a significant growth in peak current (2.67 to 5.05 A g−1).
The Tafel slope of reduction peak R2 for Li─S cells with 60DTL was 63.96 mV dec−1, while the Tafel slope of cells with 0DTL was 95.15 mV dec−1 (Figure 4c).
The lower Tafel slopes demonstrate faster reaction kinetics for the Li2S deposition process.
The CV mode contour plots of the Li─S cells at different scan rates and their corresponding CV curves are shown in Figure 4d,e, and Figure S16, Supporting Information.
The redox peaks of Li2S deposition and decomposition both show significantly enhanced current response with increasing sweep rate in 60DTL electrolyte (Figure 4d).
In addition to this, the yellow contour curves of redox peaks in Figure 4e show that the peak width of 0DTL electrolyte increases significantly with increasing sweep rate.
In comparison, the 60DTL electrolyte can also maintain a sharp peak shape at high sweep speeds, and the area of the contour curves is significantly reduced.
The significant acceleration of the Li2S decomposition process is attributed to the modulation of the product deposition morphology.

Conclusion In conclusion, this work demonstrated a clustered polysulfide encapsulation mechanism through a novel electrolyte composed of 1,2-dimethylbenzene (DTL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME).
Both computational and experimental results elucidate the aggregation behavior of polysulfides in 60DTL electrolytes under the regulation of TFSI−.

The clustered polysulfides, as new active species, modulate the reaction mechanism of lithium–sulfur batteries, enhancing the lithium sulfide deposition process and enabling 3D lithium sulfide deposition.
Furthermore, the solubility of polysulfides is finely regulated, leading to significant suppression of the shuttle effect and effective stabilization of the lithium anode.

As a result, the CPE electrolyte exhibits improved electrochemical performance than conventional DOL/DME-based electrolytes, and the rate performance and cycling stability of the battery are significantly improved, with smooth operation under lean electrolyte conditions.

This work not only presents an alternative polysulfide-conversion mechanism via a new electrolyte system with excellent reaction kinetics and anode stability for Li─S batteries but also elucidates the critical role of polysulfide dissolution behavior in governing sulfur redox reactions.
These findings provide valuable insights into the complex sulfur conversion process and offer a significant advancement in the understanding of Li─S battery chemistry.

All the electrochemical tests were performed on Neware multichannel battery cycler. 1.5 Computational Details To simulate CE and CPE electrolyte systems over 17,000 atoms, we employed machine learning potentials for molecular dynamics (MLMD) simulations.
The initial configurations of Li2S4, LiTFSI, DME, THF and DTL were optimized using Gaussian09 program with M062X/6-311+G(d,p).
The CE and CPE electrolyte systems were prepared by randomly placing the molecules in the simulation box based on their experimental densities and molar ratios.
For CE electrolyte (0DTL electrolyte), 120 LiTFSI, 74 THF, 738 DME and 30 Li2S4 molecules were added to the simulation box (60*60*60 Å3).
For CPE electrolyte (60DTL electrolyte), 120 LiTFSI, 74 THF, 272 DME, 596 DTL and 30 Li2S4 molecules were added to the simulation box (60*60*60 Å3).

The density functional theory (DFT) dataset was generated through an iterative workflow, which can be outlined as follows: (1) Initial MD Sampling: We initiated the process by performing MLMD simulations on simplified structures comprising approximately 300 atoms.
Each MLMD simulation was conducted for 20 ps with a time step of 0.5 fs.
(2) Model Training: Two independent models, differing only in their initial random seeds, were trained concurrently to assess the robustness of the predictions.
(3) Error Evaluation: After each MLMD simulation, the forces on the sampled structures were predicted using both models.
Structures with prediction errors exceeding 0.2 eV/Å between the two models were identified as poorly represented by the potential model and added to a temporary dataset for further processing.
(4) Dataset Augmentation: The temporary dataset was analyzed using SOAP[1] descriptors and K-means[2] clustering to extract up to 300 structurally distinct configurations.
These configurations were subjected to DFT calculations, and the resulting data were incorporated into the training dataset to enhance model accuracy.
(5) Iteration: The updated models were then used to perform another round of MLMD simulations.
Steps (3) and (4) were repeated iteratively—MLMD simulation, error evaluation, and dataset augmentation—until the prediction errors of both models were sufficiently minimized.
For the simulations, we employed the M3GNet model[3] with radial and three-body interaction cutoffs set to 5 Å and 4 Å, respectively.
The loss function was formulated as a weighted sum of mean squared errors for energies, forces, and stresses, each assigned an equal weight of 1.
A batch size of 4 was utilized, along with an exponential learning rate scheduler initialized at 110-3.
The convergence criteria for training were set stringently, requiring forces to fall below 0.1 eV/Å.
Training was performed on a Tesla A100 GPU until validation errors converged.
After training the potential function model, we performed molecular dynamics simulations on CE and CPE electrolyte systems comprising over 17,000 atoms.
The simulations were carried out under NVT ensemble conditions, with the temperature maintained at 300 K, a time step of 0.5 fs, and a total simulation time of 30 ps.
The initial 10 ps were designated as the pre-equilibration phase.
In addition, ESPs of molecules were calculated with Gaussian09 program at the B3LYP/def2tzvp level and visualized by GaussView.

In the 60DTL electrolyte, due to the encapsulation effect of DTL, the lithium atoms in Li2S4 bonds with oxygen in TFSI− anions and aggregates to form a cluster state.
As a result, the free lithium polysulfide molecules are drastically reduced, and the polysulfides aggregate with TFSI− anions to form the CPE species.
In addition, significantly elongated S-S bonds in Li2S4 molecule (S2-S3 atoms labeled in the Figure S4 and S5) were observed in the CPE species.
According to our previous report,[4] the S-S bond at the center of Li2Sn is most easily broken, and thus the bond length of the central S-S bond determines its reactive properties.
We compared the bond lengths of S2-S3 in the cluster polysulfide species in the CPE electrolyte with those in the free lithium polysulfide in the CE electrolyte, as shown in the above Figure.
The stretching of the central S-S bonds in CPE species may be related to the mediation of TFSI−.

The binding between lithium atom of polysulfides and the O atom of TFSI− increases the negative charge in polysulfides, leading to enhanced electrostatic repulsion between sulfur atoms, which in turn leads to a stretching of the central S-S bond.

The bond lengths of the S2-S3 bonds of Li2S4 molecules were elongated from 1.95-2.45 Å to 2.45-2.85 Å, indicating that the Li2S4 molecules in the CPE species were activated and the reactivity was enhanced.
